00:00 - 00:02: A sustained high-pitched tone.
00:02 - 00:04: A male voice asks, "What is Nirvana?"
00:04 - 00:07: Silence.
00:07 - 00:20: The same male voice speaks: "Nirvana is when everything the mind makes comes to a stop, the letting go of everything carried, the thirst ends, nothing pulls you anymore, stopping, going out, like a flame with no fuel."
00:20 - 00:21: Silence.
00:21 - 00:34: A different male voice with an accent and lower recording quality begins: "This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely, the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction."
00:34 - 00:38: Silence with background hiss.
00:38 - 01:29: The accented voice continues: "The simile of the extinction of a fire is very often brought in as an illustration of Nibbana. In the Aggivacchagotta Sutta of the Majjhima Nikaya, we find the Buddha presenting it as a sustained simile, giving it a deeper philosophical dimension. Now when a fire burns, it does so with the help of firewood. When a fire is burning, if someone were to ask us what is burning, what shall we say as a reply? Is it the wood that is burning, or the fire that is burning? The truth of the matter is that the wood burns because of the fire and the fire burns because of the wood. So it seems we already have here a case of relatedness of this to that, idappaccayata. This itself shows that there's a very deep significance in the fire simile. Nibbana as a term for the ultimate aim of this Dhamma is equally significant because of its allusion to the going out of a fire. In the Asankhata Samyutta of the Samyutta Nikaya, as many as 33 terms are listed to denote this ultimate aim. But out of all these epithets, Nibbana became the most widely used, probably because of its significant allusion to the fire. The fire simile holds the answer to many questions relating to the ultimate goal. The wandering ascetic Vacchagotta, as well as many others, accused the Buddha of teaching a doctrine of annihilation. Saro sattassa ucchedam vinassam vibhavam pannyati."
01:29: A thump sound.
01:30 - 01:34: Silence.
01:34 - 02:00: The accented voice resumes: "There seems to be some contradiction in the commentarial definitions of Nibbana. On the one hand we have the definition of Nibbana as the exit from craving which is called a weaving. And on the other it is said that it is on seeing Nibbana that craving is destroyed. To project Nibbana into a distance and to hope that craving will be destroyed only on seeing it is something like trying to build a staircase to a palace one cannot yet see. In fact this is a simile which the Buddha had used in his criticism of the Brahmin's point of view."
